mainEntity.name: Will sleeping on my implant side cause it to fail?

acceptedAnswer.text: Occasionally sleeping on the implant side is unlikely to cause implant failure on its own, particularly if the implant is well-placed and healing is progressing normally. However, repeated or prolonged pressure on the surgical site in the first two weeks is best avoided as a general precaution. Implant failure is typically related to factors such as infection, bone quality, smoking, or uncontrolled systemic conditions rather than sleeping position alone. If you are concerned about your recovery, contact your dental team for reassurance.

mainEntity.name: How much swelling is normal after dental implant surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some degree of swelling is entirely expected following any oral surgical procedure. It typically peaks around 48–72 hours after surgery before gradually reducing over the following days. Applying a cold compress to the outside of your face in the first 24 hours can help manage swelling. If swelling continues to worsen after the third day, or if it is accompanied by increasing pain or fever, it is advisable to contact your dental team for an assessment.

mainEntity.name: Can I use a regular pillow after dental implant surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no requirement to use a special pillow, but elevating your head above chest level with an extra standard pillow is generally helpful in the first few days. The goal is gentle elevation to assist fluid drainage and reduce swelling. Some patients find a wedge pillow helpful for maintaining this position comfortably through the night without rolling flat.

mainEntity.name: When can I return to my normal sleeping position?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many patients feel comfortable returning to their preferred sleeping position after two to four weeks, depending on how their healing has progressed. If you had additional procedures such as a bone graft or sinus lift, your dental team may advise a longer period of caution. Always follow the individual aftercare guidance provided by your dental surgeon rather than a general timeframe alone.

Sleeping position is unlikely to directly affect osseointegration, which is primarily influenced by bone quality, implant stability at placement, oral hygiene, and systemic health factors. However, maintaining a comfortable and stable recovery environment — including appropriate sleeping position — supports the broader healing process that osseointegration is part of. Disturbing the surgical site through pressure or trauma in the early weeks is simply an unnecessary risk worth avoiding.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal to feel the implant site when lying on that side?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some awareness of the surgical site when pressure is applied, particularly in the early weeks, is not unusual. The area will be healing and may feel tender or slightly different from surrounding tissue. This awareness often reduces as healing progresses. If you notice sharp pain, unusual movement, or any sensation that concerns you, speaking with your dental team is always the appropriate step.
